precepts.text: Nebuchadnezzar carried the real king Jehoiachin to Babylon and made his father's brother Mattaniah king in his stead, changing his name to Zedekiah, a puppet king set up by the oppressor.
precepts.point: Zedekiah was not of the royal lineage per se, and Zedekiah was not really his name; to see how he became king we go back to when Babylon took the real king away.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
To see how Zedekiah became king, go back to when Babylon took the real king away. Nebuchadnezzar “carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, and the king’s mother, and the king’s wives, and his officers, and the mighty of the land”, with “all the men of might, even seven thousand, and craftsmen and smiths a thousand, all that were strong and apt for war”.

Then “the king of Babylon made Mattaniah his father’s brother king in his stead, and changed his name to Zedekiah.” So Zedekiah was not of the royal lineage per se, and Zedekiah was not really his name. He was Mattaniah, the real king's father's brother, a puppet king set up by the oppressor. That is the Zedekiah who “was one and twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.”

precepts.text: The whole land would be a desolation and these nations would serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and only then would the Most High punish Babylon for their iniquity.
precepts.point: The Most High had told through Jeremiah that the people would have to serve Babylon seventy years, but Zedekiah decided to rebel against it instead of submitting to the prophecy.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
The Most High had already told through Jeremiah what the people would have to do: “this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.” And only when the seventy years were accomplished would he “punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the Lord, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations.”

Zedekiah decided to rebel against Babylon instead of submitting to the prophecy. He did that which was evil in the eyes of the Most High as Jehoiakim had done, and through the anger of the Most High against Jerusalem and Judah, “Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.” The seventy years of service had been declared; rebelling against Babylon was rebelling against the word.

precepts.text: These curses are a sign upon us and upon our seed forever because we served not the Most High with joyfulness and gladness of heart.
precepts.point: This should sound familiar; the same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D. These are generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
“And they shall be upon thee for a sign and for a wonder, and upon thy seed for ever.” These curses are a sign upon us and upon our seed forever because we served not the Most High with joyfulness and gladness of heart.

That is why the siege of Jerusalem should sound familiar. Nebuchadnezzar and all his army pitched against the city and built forts round about it, and the famine was so sore “that there was no bread for the people of the land.” The same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D. These are generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments: upon thee, and upon thy seed for ever.

precepts.text: The Most High would bring a nation from far, swift as the eagle, of fierce countenance, to besiege the gates and destroy the food until the people ate the flesh of their own sons and daughters.
precepts.point: This should sound familiar; the same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D. These are generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
The siege was written before it happened. “The Lord shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the end of the earth, as swift as the eagle flieth; a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand; A nation of fierce countenance, which shall not regard the person of the old, nor shew favour to the young”.

That nation eats “the fruit of thy cattle, and the fruit of thy land, until thou be destroyed”, leaving neither corn, wine, nor oil. “And he shall besiege thee in all thy gates, until thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst, throughout all thy land”. The food is destroyed until “thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the Lord thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee”.

That is what Nebuchadnezzar and all his army did: they came against Jerusalem, pitched against it, built forts round about, and besieged it until the eleventh year of Zedekiah, until the famine was so sore there was no bread for the people of the land. And the same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D.; these are generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments.

precepts.text: That same mighty and ancient nation, whose language we knew not, would eat up our harvest, bread, flocks, and herds, and it came to pass with the Chaldeans.
precepts.point: This should sound familiar; the same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D. These are generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
Jeremiah himself had told them: “Lo, I will bring a nation upon you from far, O house of Israel, saith the Lord: it is a mighty nation, it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language thou knowest not, neither understandest what they say.” “Their quiver is as an open sepulchre, they are all mighty men.”

That same nation would “eat up thine harvest, and thy bread, which thy sons and thy daughters should eat: they shall eat up thy flocks and thine herds: they shall eat up thy vines and thy fig trees: they shall impoverish thy fenced cities, wherein thou trustedst, with the sword.” It came to pass with the Chaldeans: Nebuchadnezzar and all his army pitched against Jerusalem and built forts round about, and by the fourth month the famine was so sore in the city that there was no bread for the people of the land.

Yet “in those days, saith the Lord, I will not make a full end with you.” And when they ask “Wherefore doeth the Lord our God all these things unto us?” the answer is given: “Like as ye have forsaken me, and served strange gods in your land, so shall ye serve strangers in a land that is not yours.” These are the generational curses that fall on multiple generations when we break the Most High's commandments, and the same siege and famine came on us again under the Romans in 70 A.D.

precepts.text: The Most High foretold He would deliver Zedekiah and the people into Nebuchadnezzar's hand, and he would smite them with the sword without pity, mercy, or sparing.
precepts.point: Then they put out Zedekiah's eyes, so the last thing he would ever see was his sons put to death in his face, and they bound him in chains, carried him to Babylon, and kept him in prison till the day of his death; the Most High allowed these heathen to bring hell into Jerusalem.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
The Most High foretold exactly what happened to Zedekiah: “I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people, and such as are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those that seek their life: and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy.”

So when the city was broken up and the men of war fled by night by the gate between the two walls, the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, his army scattered from him. They brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, “where he gave judgment upon him.” No pity, no mercy, no sparing: the king of Babylon “slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes” and slew all the princes of Judah in Riblah.

Then they put out Zedekiah's eyes, so the last thing he would ever see was his sons put to death in his face, bound him in chains, carried him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death. The Most High allowed these heathen to bring hell into Jerusalem, just as he said.

precepts.text: The Most High would bring the people and their king into a nation neither they nor their fathers had known, to serve other gods of wood and stone.
precepts.point: Then they put out Zedekiah's eyes, so the last thing he would ever see was his sons put to death in his face, and they bound him in chains, carried him to Babylon, and kept him in prison till the day of his death; the Most High allowed these heathen to bring hell into Jerusalem.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
“The Lord shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known; and there shalt thou serve other gods, wood and stone.” The people and their king together, carried into a nation they had never known.

That is Zedekiah bound in chains and carried to Babylon, kept in prison till the day of his death, after the king of Babylon slew his sons before his eyes and put out his eyes. The Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho, his army scattered from him, and brought him up to Riblah in the land of Hamath for judgment. The Most High allowed these heathen to bring hell into Jerusalem, because he had said the king they set over themselves would go with them into that strange nation.

precepts.text: Not only the Chaldeans but the Edomites took part in burning the temple when Judea was made desolate.
precepts.point: Edom were Babylon's personal cheerleaders, calling for Jerusalem and the temple to be razed to the foundation; the daughter of Babylon that Edom cheered on became the mother of harlots, Babylon the great, which is to be destroyed.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
“Thou also hast vowed to build up the temple, which the Edomites burned when Judea was made desolate by the Chaldees.” Not only the Chaldeans but the Edomites took part in burning the temple when Judea was made desolate.

So when Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard “burned the house of the Lord, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem”, the Chaldeans birthed this destruction, but Edom, the so-called white man, took part in it. Esau loves burning things, which is ironic since he is destined to burn forever, wasted away by the same fire he loved to waste these nations with.

precepts.text: Remember the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation, and happy shall he be that rewardeth Babylon as she served us.
precepts.point: Edom were Babylon's personal cheerleaders, calling for Jerusalem and the temple to be razed to the foundation; the daughter of Babylon that Edom cheered on became the mother of harlots, Babylon the great, which is to be destroyed.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
“Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.” Edom were Babylon's personal cheerleaders, calling for Jerusalem and the temple to be razed to the foundation, while Nebuzaradan burned the house of the Lord and the king's house and all the houses of the great men, and the army of the Chaldeans broke down all the walls of Jerusalem round about.

Then the psalm turns: “O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us. Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones.” The daughter of Babylon that Edom cheered on became the mother of harlots, Babylon the great, which is to be destroyed. Happy shall he be that rewards her as she served us.

precepts.text: Because Hezekiah showed Babylon all his treasures, the days would come when all in his house would be carried to Babylon and nothing would be left.
precepts.point: This was a billion dollar heist of the temple's gold, brass, and silver, and it too was prophecy; it fulfilled what was foretold to Hezekiah when he foolishly showed Babylon all his treasures.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
Hezekiah foolishly showed Babylon all his treasures, and Isaiah told him: “Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord. And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”

That is what Nebuzaradan finished. The Chaldeans broke the pillars of brass, the bases, and the brazen sea in the house of the Most High and carried all the brass to Babylon, along with the caldrons, shovels, snuffers, bowls, spoons, and every vessel of brass, gold, and silver; “that which was of gold in gold, and that which was of silver in silver, took the captain of the guard away.” Nothing was left. This was a billion dollar heist of the temple's gold, brass, and silver, and it too was prophecy.

precepts.text: The Most High would take away from Jerusalem and Judah the whole stay of bread and water, and the mighty man, the man of war, the judge, the prophet, and the counselor.
precepts.point: Babylon made sure to put our mighty men to death, the same tactic the oppressor always used in slavery and segregation, killing the mightiest men to destroy the people's hope so they would no longer rise up against the enemy.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
“For, behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, doth take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread, and the whole stay of water, The mighty man, and the man of war, the judge, and the prophet, and the prudent, and the ancient, The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator.”

That is the list Nebuzaradan took: Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, the three keepers of the door, the eunuch over the men of war, seven of the king's counselors, the principal scribe, and threescore men of the people found in the city. He brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and the king smote them and put them to death, “Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land.”

Babylon made sure to put our mighty men to death. It is the same tactic the oppressor always used in slavery and segregation, killing the mightiest men to destroy the people's hope so they would no longer rise up against the enemy.
